title: Halal Barbecue Is Taking Over Texas, One Brisket at a Time
summary:
At 9 a.m. on a scorching Saturday, nearly 100 people were already lined up outside Goldee's BBQ in Fort Worth, Texas. Thanh Huynh, 30, had been there since 6:30 a.m., ready to spend "lots of money" on meats and sides. The sweet, smoky scent of barbecue filled the air.

But Goldee's isn't your typical Texas joint. It's one of at least a dozen barbecue spots across the state serving halal meats—food prepared according to Islamic law. For Muslims like Haris Ghaffar, who drove an hour from Celina, this is a game-changer. "Now there are so many options, and for us to have highly rated barbecue, it's a blessing," he said.

Growing up in the 1990s, Ghaffar said a McDonald's Filet-O-Fish was one of the few halal meals he could eat out. Today, halal food is a multibillion-dollar industry. Food writer Farhan Mustafa, who covered the trend for Bon Appétit, puts it simply: "Halal food is American food."

These Muslim pitmasters are adding inventive twists to classic Texas barbecue. Zain Shafi, co-owner of Goldee's, brought tandoori smoked turkey to the menu, drawing on his Pakistani heritage. At Kafi BBQ in Irving, owner Salahodeen Abdul-Kafi—a former Silicon Valley tech worker—serves 13-spice Wagyu brisket, pomegranate-glazed beef belly burnt ends, and Iraqi-inspired spicy beef sausage.

Abdul-Kafi moved to Texas six years ago seeking a Muslim community. He started smoking brisket in his backyard, and by 2024, he opened Kafi BBQ. He attributes his obsession with quality to the Islamic concept of "Ihsan"—doing something with excellence for the sake of God.

Customers are taking notice. Jonathan Tate, a Fort Worth resident, called the sausage "the top sausage I've ever had." Abdul-Kafi's goal is bold: "To make the best barbecue in Texas." And he's not shy about it. "Making the best barbecue in Texas does not necessarily have to include pork," he says.

As these pitmasters blend tradition with innovation, they're proving that Texas barbecue is for everyone.
why_it_matters: Food is one of the most visible ways culture changes, and a halal restaurant that takes on Texas barbecue shows how religious practice and regional tradition can strengthen each other. For teenagers, it is a reminder that including different communities often creates something new and exciting rather than simply dividing people.

background_read: Texas barbecue traditionally means beef brisket slow-cooked for hours until smoky and tender, with pork ribs and sausages also part of the style.
Halal food follows Islamic law: no pork is allowed, and meat must come from permissible animals slaughtered in the proper way.
Over several decades, the U.S. Muslim population has grown, turning halal food into a multibillion-dollar industry rather than a small specialty request.
Goldee's in Fort Worth and Kafi BBQ in Irving are part of a wave of at least a dozen Texas halal barbecue spots where Muslim pitmasters add flavors from their own backgrounds.
Bon Appétit, where food writer Farhan Mustafa covered the trend, is a major American food magazine; he argues that halal food is American food.

perspectives.description: Muslim barbecue fans gain real choices: instead of defaulting to a fish sandwich, they can eat award-level brisket and sausage made according to their faith. Ghaffar's word for this is 'blessing.'
Some barbecue traditionalists may see a pork-free menu as a break from Texas convention. Abdul-Kafi's answer is direct: making the best barbecue in Texas does not necessarily have to include pork.

This story fits a historical American pattern: immigrant cooks borrow a regional favorite and expand its audience. A decade ago, halal barbecue was rare; now it is covered by major food magazines and pulls customers from an hour away.

If demand keeps growing, more halal-certified meat suppliers, restaurant competitions, and barbecue styles may follow. The trend could also push other classic American foods to think about religious inclusion.
